implementation_notes: Codable conformance is synthesized by the compiler (or written by hand for awkward fields) and Foundation's JSONEncoder/JSONDecoder do the conversion, so the graph becomes Data or a String that the persistence layer binds to a text/blob column (Core Data/SwiftData transformable attribute, GRDB, or the SQLite C API). The payload is opaque to the store, so pin CodingKeys and keep a format version alongside it.
pitfalls: Codable keys default to the property names, so renaming a property makes old payloads fail to decode unless CodingKeys are pinned and new fields are optional with defaults.
Date and Data properties use default encoding strategies (deferredToDate, base64); encoder and decoder must agree or a round trip silently changes values.
Reading stored archives with NSKeyedUnarchiver requires secure coding with an explicit class list; unarchiving arbitrary data is an insecure-deserialization trap.

variants.name: NSKeyedArchiver blob (Core Data transformable)
variants.implementation_notes: The Objective-C era route survives in Core Data: an attribute marked transformable stores an NSKeyedArchiver archive of the object graph, with NSSecureCoding and an explicit class list providing some safety on read. Choose it when an existing Core Data model already stores the graph this way or when the graph contains types that do not implement Codable; new designs should prefer Codable plus JSON.
pitfalls: Keyed archives embed class names, so a module or class rename breaks decoding of existing blobs and the archive is effectively a private format.
requiringSecureCoding with an explicit class allow-list is mandatory for safety; without it the unarchiver will happily instantiate whatever the blob names.
